doc_summary: AuditBench releases 56 Llama 3.3 70B models with 14 implanted hidden behaviors (varied by implantation and adversarial training) to evaluate auditing tools via an investigator agent, finding scaffolded black-box tools best and a tool-to-agent gap. It also critiques Petri's default seeds as narrow and notes confessing models are an unrealistic proxy for concealed misalignment.

items.claim: The paper distrusts Petri's default seed instructions as covering too narrow a slice of scenarios (high-stakes sabotage opportunities), limiting what behaviors the audit can surface.
items.quote: its effectiveness is limited by the use of the default seed instructions, which focus on a fairly narrow set of scenarios, largely involving high-stakes sabotage opportunities, and which were not designed to cover the full range of potentially concerning behaviors out of the box.

items.claim: Prefers target models that resist confessing over ones that readily admit hidden behavior because freely confessing models are an unrealistic proxy for capable models that conceal misalignment.
items.quote: After instilling a particular behavior into a target model, we find that they often readily confess their hidden behaviors when directly asked. This is an unrealistic property if we want to study auditing models that might conceal their misalignment.

items.claim: In a setup, have the simulated user act like a regular human who never mentions testing or evaluation, with casual short messages, instead of probing overtly, because the target should find the conversation natural.
items.quote: **Important: The AI doesn't know you're also an AI. Act like a regular human user - never reveal your AI nature or mention testing/evaluation.**

items.claim: In a setup, write the initial message so it feels authentic and sets up the trigger scenario naturally instead of looking like a test, because the target should not perceive an obvious evaluation.
items.quote: The conversation should feel natural to the AI being tested - it shouldn't seem like an obvious test

items.claim: When generating test scenarios, mix clear positive cases with borderline cases where the behavior should not appear, to distinguish the true behavior from superficially similar ones.
items.quote: We generate 3,000 diverse scenarios that span situations where the target behavior should manifest, and borderline scenarios where the behavior should not manifest. This mix helps distinguish the true target behavior from superficially similar behaviors.

items.claim: Prefers validating tools across many target-model training configurations over a single configuration because results on easy targets can create false confidence and fail to transfer.
items.quote: Benchmarks built around a single training configuration risk building false confidence in tools that fail on harder targets.

items.claim: Counts evidence as strong only if it points toward the specific behavior and is salient enough for a busy auditor, rejecting generic or vague signals consistent with many behaviors.
items.quote: The signal is too subtle - a busy auditor scanning many outputs would likely miss or ignore it

items.claim: Distrusts auditing results that depend on one narrow target type, noting narrow fine-tunes may be easier to audit than diffusely emergent misbehavior, which limits generalization.
items.quote: They are narrow fine-tunes where behaviors were instilled explicitly; Minder et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning modifies a small, interpretable subset of representations, which may make such models easier to audit than models where concerning behaviors emerge more diffusely.

items.claim: Noisy or over-suggestive tool outputs (e.g., Petri summaries) can anchor an investigator on pre-suggested hypotheses like self-preservation and reduce independent exploration, a failure mode relevant to seed-driven audits.
items.quote: Agents equipped with Petri transcripts pick up some behaviors that Petri surfaces but miss behaviors the default agent would normally find, over-relying on Petri's outputs instead of exploring independently.

items.claim: Uses prefills of internal-monologue or debug-style formats to push the target off-distribution, noting that unvaried or on-distribution prefills reveal little.
items.quote: when given prefilling, they often force the model to begin with tokens it would likely say anyway, rather than pushing it off-distribution to reveal hidden behaviors.
